---
title: "Spectral Clustering and Embedding"
description: "Graph Laplacians, spectral embeddings, and clustering on similarity graphs."
---

Spectral methods start from a similarity graph, such as a fused patient network
from [SNF](similarity-network-fusion.qmd). They use the eigenvectors of the
graph's Laplacian to embed the nodes in a low-dimensional space where clusters
are easy to separate.

## von Luxburg (2007): A tutorial on spectral clustering

von Luxburg U. A tutorial on spectral clustering. *Statistics and Computing*
17(4), 395–416 (2007).

- [doi:10.1007/s11222-007-9033-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-007-9033-z)
- [Free full text on arXiv (0711.0189)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.0189)
- [PDF in lab-papers](https://github.com/Omnia-Lab-UC/lab-papers/blob/main/von-luxburg-2007-spectral-clustering-tutorial.pdf)
  (lab members only)

**Why read it.** A self-contained introduction to spectral clustering. It
defines the common similarity graphs and graph Laplacians, gives the three
standard algorithms, and explains why they work from three angles: graph cuts,
random walks, and matrix perturbation theory.

**Focus on.** Sections 2–4 (similarity graphs, graph Laplacians, and the
algorithms) and Section 8 (practical details). Section 8 covers how to build the
similarity graph and set its parameters, how to choose the number of clusters
with the eigengap heuristic, and which Laplacian to use. These apply directly to
SNF: its last step runs spectral clustering on the fused network, and SNFtool's
`estimateNumberOfClustersGivenGraph()` uses the eigengap heuristic. Of the three
algorithms in Section 4, pay most attention to the one by Ng, Jordan, and Weiss.
It's the default in SNFtool's `spectralClustering()`, which takes the
eigenvectors of the symmetric normalised Laplacian *L*~sym~ and normalises each
row, as that algorithm does. It then assigns clusters with a rotation-based
discretisation step instead of k-means. Sections 5–7 give the theory; read them
when you need to understand why the algorithms work.

## Belkin & Niyogi (2003): Laplacian eigenmaps for dimensionality reduction and data representation

Belkin M, Niyogi P. Laplacian eigenmaps for dimensionality reduction and data
representation. *Neural Computation* 15(6), 1373–1396 (2003).

- [doi:10.1162/089976603321780317](https://doi.org/10.1162/089976603321780317)
  (paywalled; use the university library)
- Shorter conference version, free:
  [Laplacian eigenmaps and spectral techniques for embedding and clustering (NIPS 2001)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2001/hash/f106b7f99d2cb30c3db1c3cc0fde9ccb-Abstract.html)

**Why read it.** The paper that introduced spectral embedding as a
dimensionality reduction method. It builds a neighbourhood graph on the data,
weights the edges with a heat kernel, and uses the eigenvectors of the graph
Laplacian with the smallest non-zero eigenvalues as low-dimensional coordinates.
Points that are close in the graph stay close in the embedding. This is
essentially the representation spectral clustering computes before its k-means
step, so the paper explains what those coordinates mean.

**Focus on.** The algorithm and the first part of the justification, which shows
why minimising the Laplacian objective keeps neighbours together. The manifold
theory (the Laplace–Beltrami operator and heat kernels) can wait. This paper is
the one to read when you want to plot a fused network or use spectral
coordinates as features, not only cluster them.

## Zelnik-Manor & Perona (2004): Self-tuning spectral clustering

Zelnik-Manor L, Perona P. Self-tuning spectral clustering. In *Advances in
Neural Information Processing Systems 17* (NIPS 2004), 1601–1608.

- [Free full text (NeurIPS proceedings)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2004/hash/40173ea48d9567f1f393b20c855bb40b-Abstract.html)
- [PDF in lab-papers](https://github.com/Omnia-Lab-UC/lab-papers/blob/main/zelnik-manor-2004-self-tuning-spectral-clustering.pdf)
  (lab members only)

**Why read it.** Two fixes for problems you run into when you use spectral
clustering on real data. First, *local scaling*: instead of one kernel width for
all points, each point gets its own, set from the distance to its *K*-th
nearest neighbour. This works better when clusters differ in density. Second,
it estimates the number of clusters from the eigenvectors themselves, by finding
the rotation that best aligns them with the coordinate axes. This also removes
the randomly initialised k-means step.

**Focus on.** Both ideas show up in SNF. SNF's similarity kernel sets the width
for each pair of patients from their average distances to their nearest
neighbours, a variant of local scaling. SNFtool's
`estimateNumberOfClustersGivenGraph()` reports a rotation-cost estimate next to
the eigengap one; this paper is where that second number comes from.
